content:
We have carbon NMR data: chemical shifts: 169.52, 132.43,130.27,129.30,126.70,126.66,123.57,43.30,26.29 ppm.

We need number of methyl (CH3) groups in the molecule. Methyl carbons appear around 10-30 ppm for aliphatic, but also 40 ppm for carbon attached to heteroatoms. Here we have peaks at 43.30 and 26.29. Likely methyl groups correspond to 26.29 (typical for CH3 attached to carbonyl? maybe). 43.30 could be a methylene or carbon attached to heteroatom (e.g., carbonyl carbon of acetyl). But we need count of CH3 groups. Could also be two methyls: one at 26.29, another at 43.30 maybe a carbonyl carbon of acetyl (CH3-CO-). Actually carbonyl carbon appears ~200 ppm, not present. 169.52 likely carbonyl (C=O of ester or amide). So 43.30 could be a carbon attached to carbonyl (e.g., CH2 of ethyl). But methyl attached to carbonyl (acetyl) appears ~30 ppm. So 26.29 likely methyl. 43.30 maybe a methylene (CH2). So likely only one methyl.

But we could also get proton NMR to confirm. Let's get proton NMR.
